utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just to clarify that a bit, sir, when you say "Dutch authorities," are you referring to questions that you were asked which referenced the NIOD, N-I-O-D, report?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, with that clarification in mind, can you further attest that if you were asked the same questions today which you were asked during the last trial in November 2006, that your answers would be the same?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: Yes, sir, you can ask the same questions and I will give the same answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution at this time tenders P00435 under seal, and P436, the Popovic testimony, the public version, being the latter exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: They will be received, the first one under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this time I would like to read the Rule 92 ter summary for this witness. We have distributed it to the parties and the booth. I apologise in advance. It's a little on the longer side. We had four days of testimony to try to condense, and given this witness's role, as I think you'll see during the course of his testimony, and the depth of his knowledge, I've tried to reduce it as much as I can. But it still came out a little longer than what we've been used to. Prior to the war, the witness was a Ham Radio enthusiast, earned a B-category Ham Radio classification, and went to various competitions. During his JNA service, he was trained as a radio telegraphist and worked in a radio centre, where his main duties were to ensure the connections for radio, teleprinter, and telegraphic connection. In the early part of the war, the witness was a member of a unit that dealt primarily with protecting the civilian population from air raids. He then became involved in intercepting aircraft communications and later set up an intercepting centre for his local army brigade. In the fall of 1993, the witness helped set up the northern location's interception site and was a member of the platoon based there until the end of the war. The witness identified the location of that site on a map. The witness's unit worked 10-day shifts at the site. He identified and discussed a list of ABiH personnel who worked at the northern site and the level of their amateur radio classification, if any. At the northern location, there was also a unit from the army's 21st Division and a MUP unit. The witness described the layout of the site, where the three units were located within the building, and was shown a sketch he drew of the layout. As far as the witness knows, there was no sharing of material between his unit and the 21st Division operators at the site, and the two units separately sent their reports to the 2nd Corps. His unit had an order to share materials with the MUP operators at the site, and the MUP operators gave the army cryptographer reports to send through as part of the army reports. The witness's unit listened mostly to the area of the Drina Corps, and he was familiar with the names of its brigades, as well as with the Main Staff, and had a map that plotted the axes and frequencies of the VRS radio-relay sets. He also discussed a list of VRS code-names. The last order his unit received to move the antennas was on 8 June 1995, and instructed them to direct the antennas towards Zvornik, Vlasenica, and the River Drina. The witness explained the procedure for intercepting, recording, transcribing and transmitting intercept conversations as follows: His unit would receive an order, which would include information such as which axis, azimuth, direction, sector, frequency or participants to monitor. His unit would turn the antennas in the appropriate direction and begin searching for the frequencies and then the participants. When they located a conversation they wanted to record, they depressed the pause button on the recorder and listened to the conversation with headphones on, noting the time, frequency and channel on a piece of paper. His unit had four sets of recorders and scanners and four corresponding note-books. After recording the conversation, the operators then began to transcribe the conversation. After recording the conversation, the operators then began to transcribe it. They would first transfer the time, frequency, and channel information from the piece of paper into the note-book, then throw the piece of paper away. They would leave some room at the top for the participants' identity, if that were not known when the operator began transcribing the conversation, and they would fill in the participants' names later if they learned them as they were playing the recording. If they did not, they marked the participants as X, Y, or Z. They then continued to transcribe the conversation by playing back the tape and transcribing three to five words or as much as they could remember hearing, then rewound the tape again to be sure, then continued with the next few words, and so on. Even though the operators had very trained ears, sometimes after listening to a portion of a conversation up to 10 times, with everyone gathered around, they still could not understand a word, so they would put dots in its place. Once the transcript was finished, the operator took the note-book to the KZ or encryption room, where the cryptographer typed up the handwritten transcript into a computer, encrypted it, and sent it by modem to the command. As far as the witness knows, the date was automatically entered by the computer in the heading of each report. The note-book was considered a draft, and the print-out the finished product and official document. The witness identified in photographs the various pieces of equipment used during this process. On the average, for a group of regular conversations, none of which was urgent, it would take up to an hour from interception of a conversation to the transmission of the intercept report to the command. A single conversation would take about 20 minutes to half an hour. If there were no urgency, the regular daily reports would be sent out between 1900 and 2100 hours. When combat operations were underway, the intercept reports had to be sent to his command as soon as possible. The witness reviewed an intercept he transcribed of a conversation on 14 July 1995 at 2102 hours and identified his handwriting without any doubt. He then explained the process by which he transcribed this particular conversation and made edits to his transcript as he listened and re-listened to the recording. He also explained various notations made within the note-book containing this intercept. He stored the completed note-books in a safe and turned them and full tapes over to his command, and does not know what happened to them after that. Now, with the usher's assistance, I would like to hand an exhibit up to the witness. Actually, two exhibits, just to save a little bit of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, you've been handed a plastic booklet containing some documents. You can ignore the documents in English. I would turn your attention to the two tabs, blue stickies number 1 and 2. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what those documents are in that booklet?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: These documents were copied from our working note-book, number 1. Let me just look at number 2. That's number 2. So first there is the handwritten text, and number 2 is one copy of our report from the computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I would just ask you to turn back to the handwritten transcript that you have there in the booklet, back to the plastic booklet, sir, you were just looking at. If you could look at tab 1, the handwritten transcript you just described to us. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what that transcript is? What is that, what is it?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: It is an intercept at the location where I worked, and this is my handwriting, which means that I noted down this intercept. The text is self-explanatory as to the participants in the conversation, how the conversation proceeded, and how we derived some information from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what is the time on that -- on your handwritten version, sir, that that conversation occurred?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: The time is 2102 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if you could flip to tab 2, to the print-out, can you tell the Trial Chamber what the date of the report is that transmitted the typed version of your handwritten intercept transcript?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: In the heading, we see two markings, "Strictly Confidential" next to the date, "1514, 45," and you see the date, "14 July 1995."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, thank you, Witness. Now, this process and this set of procedures that you testified about in Blagojevic, as well as in the Popovic case, for intercepting, recording, transcribing, and transmitting these intercepts, did you personally follow those procedures as a matter of regular practice when you were at the northern site?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: Yes, sir, with one small exception. There's just one more small detail in question. When you press pause, the device starts recording. The rest of the procedure is described correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. While we're on that topic, let's just follow up with a couple of questions so we know exactly what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, may I interrupt you shortly. We received a booklet with hard copies. You referred to tab 1 and 2. We don't have any little blue sticks with numbers, so that it would be helpful if you could indicate the P number marked for identification in the document list which is contained in this booklet.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Will do, Mr. President. In your booklet, Mr. President, there are no dividers. It's considered as one intercept, and the translation, the English version, is P16.1. And we're going to be spending some time in a moment looking at those. And the original handwritten version is P00016.2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, back to the tape-recorder's pause button. You testified about this to some degree previously, Witness. Can you describe for the Trial Chamber exactly what you mean when you say that when you wanted to record a conversation, you had to press the pause button? And it may be helpful to describe for the Trial Chamber in what position the pause button was most of the time.

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The pause button was pressed while we were waiting to come across a conversation. The record button, the play button, and the pause button were pressed simultaneously, and the device was on standby. As soon as you pressed the pause button, the device starts recording after a very, very short delay, and it would start recording very soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. So is it fair to describe it as follows: The tape-recorder basically stayed in a position such that the pause button, if I can describe it this way, was in a down position, and if you wanted to start recording, you had to push down on that pause button, which was already in a depressed position, so that it would pop back up and begin recording?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: From what I can remember, the buttons were thin and protruding, so that you could also depress it from the bottom up, and this is what they did. With the pause button, we would push it up from below so that it would jump up quickly, so that you could start recording as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Witness. Back to the procedures that you described in terms of taking these intercepts down and transmitting them. In your experience at that northern site, did your colleagues follow those procedures as a matter of regular practice as well?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: Yes, we did follow those procedures, with some slight, perhaps, individual deviations. But generally speaking, the procedure was the same with everybody, but there were some tiny differences which are always there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, focusing your attention on the handwritten intercept that you have in your booklet and the print-out that was created from it, can you give the Trial Chamber, sir, an estimate -- I know it's going back a ways, so I'm not going to ask you for a specific time-period, but can you give the Trial Chamber an estimate, based on your experience, of how soon after that conversation was picked up by your equipment did you begin transcribing that conversation?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: From the time the conversation took place up to the time it was transcribed, an hour would go by, approximately, probably because there was some other conversations underway so we were not able to transcribe it right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, focusing on the print-out, can you give the Trial Chamber some idea of how long it took to convert your handwritten transcript into the print-out so that it could be sent out? And, again, I'm not going to demand a specific time-period, but if you can tell the Trial Chamber, was it hours, was it days? How long did it take?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: After waiting for the transcription, transcribing it from the audio to the written version, then the text would be typed into the computer, which is what you're asking about. As far as an average conversation was concerned, to transfer it from the note-book to the computer, it wouldn't take more than 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you give the Trial Chamber an idea of when that was done, in terms of when the conversation was actually picked up by your equipment? We understand that it might have taken 20 minutes to create the transcript, but in relation to when you took the conversation off the air, as it were, can you give the Trial Chamber how long it would have -- it took to get the print-out completed and then sent to your command?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: After midnight, I think, two to two and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Witness. Now, if you would kindly put the booklet down, I want to turn your attention to the other exhibit which you were handed a moment ago. And we're going to look at that both in the original version but also in e-court, and that's P00425. And if you could tell the Trial Chamber what you have in your hands, please.

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: I have the document in front of me, and it's easier to follow when I have it in front of me. This is a working note-book from my unit. It was produced in my unit during the period that we are talking about. The note-book shows that I wrote myself, in my own hand, "RRU 1," and it was intended for the monitoring of radio-relay equipment with one channel. And the number "29-2" would indicate there were a number of note-books marked with the number 29. This note-book was also entered by my own hand. When we open the note-book, on the first page, report book "RRU 1, ICR," is also text I wrote in my own hand. Then we have the following page, where we see a text which states "Strictly Confidential."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot see the original on screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What I'd like you to do is, at this point, watch the monitor, and I'd like to hand up that original note-book to the Trial Chamber, with the usher's assistance. And if we could just go back one page in e-court, please. Okay. And we've got 00779618 on the screen, just for the record. You're identifying your handwriting, I believe, sir, "RRU 1" and "29," is that correct, on the cover of this note-book?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next page, please, in e-court. And this is 00779619.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Whose handwriting is this on this page, and what does it say?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: It states "Book of reports," "RRU 1," "ICR 100," dated "26 June 1995, until," and then we have dots. This means that this is supposed to be the report book of the one channel RRU 1 ICR device, meaning that there was another note-book for a different piece of equipment. The date means that I had the book at my disposal at the time. Actually, I made it available, which means that it could start to begin to be used from the 26th of June. I had the intention of writing the other date as well, but it was a slip, so it didn't get noted. But the second date would indicate up until what time-period this note-book would be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Can we go to the next page in e-court, and this will be the opposite side in the original note-book of the page we just looked at, the flip side.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There's some notations in the upper right-hand corner of 00779620. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what these notations are and who put them there?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: This information was entered by the person in charge of supplies, who brought material to us at the facilities. Sometime -- actually, at one time I actually saw him entering this into the note-books. I assume that this is his handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And so what does that date reflect, sir?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: The entered date is the date when the note-book was recorded in the warehouse as a document, meaning that it was available to be taken to the facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just so that there is no question about this in the record, Witness, I think in response to one of my earlier questions, when you first looked at the original note-book in your hands, you identified it as something that was produced in your unit, and I just want to clarify. Did you mean that that note-book was manufactured in your unit or did you mean something else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could the usher please give the note-book to Mr. Tolimir and Mr. Gajic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, we did not produce the note-books. The contents in the note-books, different information beginning from the one we covered, from the cover page, the text inside, and other data, this is what I meant to say, and I apologise if there were any problems because of what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: [B/C/S spoken], Witness. If we can go to the next page in e-court, and if we could rotate that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We see a number 1 at the upper right-hand corner of this page. Do you see that, sir, on your screen?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And if we can go to the next page, which would be the opposite side of the current page.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do we see any number there?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't see one.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So now if we go to the next page, do you see the number 2 in the upper right-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we could go to page 108 in e-court. For the record, this is ERN 0077-9725.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There's some handwritten notation in the upper right-hand corner. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what that says and what it means, please?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: I apologise. Before I begin, can I just ask if I can read the whole text? Are we in private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes. What you can do is read the text, but without identifying any names that might be there. And if you do see a name, if you can just tell who it is, and we need to not broadcast this.

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: Very well. The heading, let me say that first, says that -- actually, when I wrote this, I received an order from the command to count the number of pages in the book, to mark them properly, and then to say what the total number of pages is in the note-book. This was done in order to prevent paper from being ripped or torn out of some note-books, so that we have a note of the total number of pages. The text says this note-book has 52 pages, platoon commander, lieutenant, and then there is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, I was told that there was no notification by the Prosecution that this is a confidential document, so that we have to redact the transcript. It was broadcast to the public gallery, but as there is nobody there, there's no harm.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We dodged that one, Mr. President. Thank you. I apologise for that lapse, and I apologise to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I just want to back up a second. The -- and we may as well go into private session for this couple of questions. I was going to do this at the end, but may as well do it now. May we go into private session, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We are going into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, we saw a moment ago, Witness, that the note-book pages --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We saw a moment ago, Witness, when you were looking at the note-book pages, that the upper right-hand corner of the pages was numbered. And if we look through the original of the whole note-book, I think we'll all agree that you will see that each of the pages was numbered through to the end. And if I could ask to get the original note-book back from Mr. Gajic, please, that would be helpful. Thank you. Would you please tell the Trial Chamber, Witness, who numbered those pages, and when were those pages numbered?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I put in those numbers and the text at the back, accompanied by my signature. Also, the previous text on page 1 and the number of the note-book on the cover were entered at the same time on the date that appears on the front page. All the markings were entered on that date that I just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And that would be on, I believe, the 21st of May, 1995. I beg your pardon. If we could just have a look at the second page of PW-435 [sic] -- I beg your pardon, 425. So we see a date here of the 26th of June, 1995. Is that when you numbered the pages, sir?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: Yes, that's the date when I entered the number on the cover and the text that we're looking at, when I put in the page numbers and this remark at the back with my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at that time, sir, had anything been recorded inside the note-book? Had any conversations been intercepted and recorded in the note-book or was it empty at that time?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: I received blank note-books, and the note-book was blank when I entered the data in it. That was the condition in order to be able to make the book available for use.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to page 88 in e-court, please. And this will be the yellow sticky number 2 on the original version before the Trial Chamber at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you see a page with the page number 43 in the upper right-hand corner, sir?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we're now looking at the intercept with a time of 2102 hours. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, whose handwriting is that, sir?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: It's my handwriting, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to the next page, and we should not broadcast the following pages, please. If we could rotate -- perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, we don't see a page number here, and is that because, sir, you only numbered the upper right-hand corner of a page within the note-book?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I think that that's what it says at the end, 52 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We see, in the upper right-hand corner, page number 44 written. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And so that we can at least stay in open session, do you see a set of two initials above the eight-digit number on this page? And if you do, whose initials are they, sir?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: Yes, sir, the initials on the left -- actually, the signature was the encryption person, indicating that the conversation was transcribed and entered into the report. The initials on the right-hand side are my initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I just want to keep your mind focused on that "44" there. And if we could have P00016.4 in e-court, please. And the translation is P00016.3. And we'll need to go to the next page of the English, please. Okay, great. Let's focus on the remark that's at the bottom of this print-out. First of all, can you explain what you are trying -- or what you were conveying here in this remark? And, secondly, is there anything that has come to your attention about this remark that you'd like to clarify or correct for the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: This note is self-evidence -- is evidently a reference to a mistake by the operator at Badem. It says this page 44 was recorded like it was the line for Jokic, which was not true. On the original document, it says "Jokic, point 44." This was a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, first can you tell the Trial Chamber whether you recall whether this remark was your remark or the cryptographer's remark?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: I wrote this remark in my own hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what we see here is that the line -- the open line that was inadvertently left open by the operator at Badem has been identified as line 44, as if that's the number of the line or the channel of communications at Badem. Let's go back very briefly and look at page 88 of P00425.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, is there any problem by mentioning in open session these words in your last question?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. We're okay for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we could just turn to -- turn two more pages to the last page of this intercept, and this should not be broadcast for the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, we're back at this last page, where we see the page number 44 written, and if you would just, for the Trial Chamber, tie up what you were explaining in terms of not referring to the error at Badem of leaving the line open, but whether there was an actual error made in the print-out version that has to do with the page number.

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Could you just explain that for the Trial Chamber, sir? What exactly was the error that was made in the print-out?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: If we look at the text, at the top, in the right top corner, we see line was open for Jokic, and there is a dot and then the number of the page. However, in retyping, this was connected and appeared as if 44 was the line for Jokic, the number of Jokic's line. But here in the original, you can see exactly what is what. The end of the sentence, full stop, and then the number of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we could go to page 109 of the note-book, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In the upper left-hand corner, we see a notation, and if you would just explain that for the Trial Chamber, please. And for the record, we're at 00779726.

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: These designations could only be recorded by someone in the warehouse. We didn't do it this way. We had a form for completing a page. I suppose that it means the day when the note-book arrived at the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And this is at the -- almost on the very last page of the note-book. So at that point, was the note-book completed, sir, was it filled?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The note-book was handed over when the shifts changed. The officer from the command would, on that occasion, hand over the used note-books, the used audiotapes, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, Witness, I don't have any further questions for you at this point. Mr. President, we have a tender list, which the Registry has compiled, giving the number of exhibits that either were admitted through this witness or are being offered to assist the Trial Chamber in making sense of -- in particular, of the Blagojevic transcript, and I can recite for the record which these exhibits are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. The exhibits which were admitted through this witness in the Popovic case are P00016.1, 16.2, 16.3, 16.4, and 16.5, P421 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it's not necessary to read out the whole list, we have it, but just indicate from which number through which number you would like to tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President. We'll have a couple of gaps. We have P421 to 423, 425 through 434, P438 and 439, and P440. And we have P424 as well. And, Mr. President, I also note that there were three exhibits which have been previously admitted, but that I would call to the Trial Chamber's attention to assist it in making sense of the Blagojevic transcript. We had them on the original tender list. I think they fell by the wayside, but I can very briefly just provide a couple citations for the Trial Chamber to assist it. P390 is an intercept note-book number 97, and we would offer pages 1 to 3. Those were shown to the witness in Popovic. Page 389 -- I'm sorry, P389 is intercept note-book 91, and we would draw the Trial Chamber's attention to page 2, which was also shown to the witness, and that was at transcript page 4407 of the Popovic trial and 4408. For the prior exhibit, that was shown to the witness at transcript pages 4410 to 4411. And P387, note-book 96, page 1 only was shown to the witness in Popovic at transcript 4408. I just draw that to the Trial Chamber's attention to make sense of the Popovic transcript. And that concludes my examination-in-chief, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The latter three exhibits are already exhibits, as you mentioned. There are seven documents. They have not yet a B/C/S translation -- or an English translation, sorry, so we will receive all those you have mentioned, but only mark for identification P424, P425, P426, P433, P438, P439, and P440.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think I made a mistake. I was now told that the three exhibits, P378, 389, 390, are not exhibits yet, but they will be assigned the numbers, and Madam Registrar will read it into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Pages 1 to 3 of Exhibit P390 is now Exhibit P465. Page 2 of Exhibit P389 is now Exhibit P466. Page 1 of P387 is now Exhibit P467. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President, if I misled the Trial Chamber. We were under the impression that they were admitted. I'm glad that's resolved. And we will liaise with the Registry when those English translations become available. I would note, for example, though, with respect to, for example, P425, that is an entire booklet of intercepts, and we typically don't translate the entire intercept booklet. It's being offered for the purposes for which we examined the witness and any other purpose the parties deem relevant, but typically we haven't been translating the entire note-books. We certainly will if the Trial Chamber instructs us, but they are numerous and they are lengthy, and many of those intercepts will not be introduced in this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, that is correct. We received this note-book, P425, as we have the original now in the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And consistent with the private session and non-broadcasting, that should be placed under seal, Mr. President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That will be under seal. Mr. Tolimir, do you have cross-examination? Before the break, we have still 10 minutes left, and you should start.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Once again, I greet all those who have not been here since this morning. I greet this witness, and wish that this trial be completed as God wills, not as I will. May I call up P434, and that is the statement of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which will not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we display page 1 in the native language of the witness, and in English in a split screen. Thank you, we can see that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question is: Witness, did you sign that statement? And if not, why not?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: First of all, good day to you, too. I did sign the English version. I didn't sign the statement on the left because I was given the statement in English. The information I provided and the details I provided I was told were written down in English. Do I want to sign it? I said, Yes. And the document shown on the left was given to me later just for my own review so that I know what the English text reflects.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, on the basis of what you just said, can I ask you whether you know the English language, and how do you know what you signed?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: I do not speak English, but the interpreter told me everything that was written here, all the details provided here, last name, first name, et cetera, and the interpreter guarantees that what I said during the interview was recorded in English on the laptop. That's how the interview was conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us why you were not given to sign your own statement in your mother tongue, and you signed the statement in English on the 12th of May, 1999?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: Yes, it's a good question. You see, I gave a statement in Bosnian. Then that statement, as such, was read out to me. Then the team, consisting of the people indicated here, told me that they want to translate this statement into English, and would I want to sign it. I said that I will sign my statement when it's translated into English from Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you stand by everything that is contained in this unsigned statement in your mother tongue? If you confirm that, then I can proceed with my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: Well, if you allow me to read it --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All that I want to ask about, I will first read out to you, and you will be able to say whether you did or did not say that. The entire statement is on eight pages, so you would need a lot of time to read it.

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: Yes, sir. You see, on the page that I'm looking at, there needs to be a small change because my current occupation changed in the meantime. Everything else is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please look at paragraph 3 of your statement. It's on page 2. Can we please see it in e-court. We can see paragraph 3, and you talk about your engagement in the BH Army. Look at the one sentence but last. You say: "During the war, it was mainly directed on providing assistance in relation to enemy activities such as evacuating the population in the event of an enemy incursion." Can you explain this practice regarding the evacuation of the population in the territory where you worked and where you worked in this Centre for Warning and Alert? What were your responsibilities, in fact?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: Yes. I was on the reserve force in this Centre for Information, Warning and Alert, and my duty was a reserve post. First, I was a signalsman in this Centre for Warning and Alert on the reserve force, and then in 1985 I completed a training course to become commander of visual observation stations in Tarcin. And upon return, we had the drills. As commander of observation post, I was trained to set up an observation post with everything that comprises, and equipment for visual observation. It was primarily aimed to serve in the case of natural disasters, but also in times of war, infantry, motorised, and other units that could be of danger to the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So you were able, independently, as an employee of that Centre for Warnings and Alert, to make that decision on evacuation, or was that decision to be made by some superior in the municipal authority?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: Since I was just commander in charge of establishing observation stations, observation posts, somebody would issue me with an order to set up a visual observation post at a certain location, and certainly all the follow-up orders would be issued accordingly, and I would comply with these orders. That means that whatever I see, and the other people manning the observation post, we would pass on. And based on the information we provide, decisions and orders would be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Would then the municipal authority decide on the evacuating the population or you, in the observation post, could decide to evacuate people?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: Yes, sir, this would be done by the relevant organ whose duties included that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you completed training in the Tarcin centre, which is outside of your hometown, is that something that applied to all the municipalities that were under the control of the B and H Army?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: I think I didn't understand the question quite clearly, but I will do my best to answer. I don't really know what the policy was in other municipalities, how it was organised. In my municipality, it was organised in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were there people in Tarcin who only worked in your municipality or were there people attending this course from other municipalities as well?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: There were people from other municipalities, but I don't know if there were people from all the municipalities attending the course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think reached the convenient time for our second break, or are you in a specific line of questions?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have just dealt with a decision on evacuation. I understood that this was done by the relevant organ, just like the witness said, and we have completed that. And we're going to move to the next group of questions when I continue my cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then we must have the second break now. We adjourn and resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can we look at P434, the statement of this witness, in e-court, please. And can we look at page 3 in the Serbian, paragraph 7. Thank you. We're moving to a different topic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, we can see that this is the last paragraph, where we're talking about the centre, your facility, and that it used to be a radar centre for the JNA before. And then you talk about the facility, itself. I would just like to ask you whether the Public Security Service listening service was located in the same facility as your own section.

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: In order to answer this question, I need to know what exactly the thrust of your question is. The State Security Service was located in the same building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was it in the same room as your service or did they have separate premises?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: No, they were not in the same room. They had their own separate room.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now see page 4, paragraph 2 of this document, so that the witness can follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This was something that was discussed in the examination-in-chief. It says: "We would record the material in the UHER apparatus, and if it was not too busy, the operator could monitor the call. If it was very busy, then he could monitor or tape another conversation at another device." Did I explain what you did very well?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When did you start to use the note-books in order to do the work you described earlier? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: In order for things to be clearer, in the beginning we had some papers, writing paper, or we used old military note-books that were a bit larger in size, and we would write the text in them. We were not asked to keep the note-books for later. As the job became more routine, then the command sent more conditions that should be met in relation to different aspects in order for our work to be more successful, and amongst other things these note-books were brought in. But I really couldn't tell you exactly when this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I don't ask for an exact date, but, approximately, if you can tell us the year and what time of the year that you had the note-books for the first time. Was it in 1994, 1995, during the first three months, the second three months? In quarterly segments, if you can tell us.

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: I couldn't really tell you the year, sir, but I can tell you that it was 1994. I really couldn't give you the exact time-period, but I can try. I'm not sure how successful I can be or how important that can be, but it's probably the second half of 1994 that we're talking about here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. So we're talking about the second half of 1994. As you said in the examination-in-chief, which dealt with this, and I don't want to repeat that, and you said earlier, that you did not keep a note down, those papers before, what did you do with that paper that you used to make your notes on?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: A small correction. We did make notes. You said we didn't make notes. You said that we made notes, because without making notes we wouldn't be able to transcribe it. The command didn't ask of us to keep them, so that's why I think we burned the papers. We used them to make a fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question is: You've seen the note-book here that the Prosecutor showed to you during the examination-in-chief, and we saw it as well. That note-book, P425, that's that exhibit, you explained the numbers that you entered into the note-book. When we look at that note-book, we can see that on page 2, it was recorded on the 26th of June, 1990 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But then you have the "21st of May, 1995," written in the note-book. Can you explain this difference in dates or do you need to see the note-books again? On the fourth page, there is no date, only the time of recording and the frequency and the number of the channel. There are no dates from the beginning to the end, except the very first date. And I looked through the whole note-book. Can you please explain why there is no date given during the listening, so that we could establish when a specific conversation was recorded? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: Of course, yes. That is a very good observation, sir. The dates were not placed -- I'm starting from the back, and then you can follow. I'm going to answer your questions in reverse order, because you put a number of questions there. During the actual transcription of the conversation, we didn't put any dates in because we were not asked to do that. Our note-book -- and our note-books, one of which you did see, was made like a kind of script, a draft, which will then later be used to make a document, and the data in the book was sufficient for us to be able to create the documents that we created and that we have now. The date that you saw, the 21st of May, I think that's what you said --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: Yes, that was the date that you mentioned, relates to the date when the note-book was constituted at the unit command, the command of the company for anti-electronic warfare of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I saw once in a dispatch that the note-books were made by the person in charge of the warehouse. He would enter these code numbers into the note-books, and then the note-books were ready to be distributed to us at the facility. For a while, they had the practice of constituting the documents in the warehouse, and then they left the warehouse and were issued to the facility. The note-book also contains other information. You would go back one page and you could see that I wrote the "26th of June, 1995." That is the date when the note-book was placed at our disposal, at the disposal of the people who worked with me, the operators. So from that date on, entries could be made into the note-book, but that doesn't mean it was immediately placed on the table, because other note-books were in use too. The third piece of data that you referred to is the number 29/2. As you said, I think it means 29 slash second copy. This is something that refers to the second copy of this particular item 29.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at P425, and can we look at page 3 in the e-court. Thank you. Can you please show page 3. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This has now been marked without stating how many pages there are in this note-book, which has been registered under number 08/201294, and so the question now is: Why was it marked, when the person who marked it did not mark the number of pages, because earlier you said that you were the one who did that, and he didn't write down how many pages there were, and he did not certify this in any way or certify it with his own signature either? Is it possible that he could have -- that the person who was actually operating the equipment could have entered this data into the note-book? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: Sir, there was no possibility that the operator entered this information into the note-book. The practice used to register documents by the command of my unit is something that you have to inquire about of the commander of that group. I cannot discuss their practice because I'm not familiar with it. What this means is that I received the document with this text already in it. I accepted it as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Since this note-book is now being used in court as an exhibit, is it logical to put the question on the basis of which can we know who wrote this, when they wrote it, who signed it, and why did they leave the possibility that the users fill in the number of pages? As users, they could have ripped out certain pages and come to the number that suited them. That's a possibility, isn't it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: These comments that you have made now, I would rather have you put them to the person who was in charge of the shift. That was the person who gave these note-books to me. Perhaps they know answers to these questions, and if not, perhaps they know who does, why this information is entered in this particular way, and why this was given to me, as such. As far as I am concerned, this is what I was given, and this is, I think, a question that should be put to the person who gave me the note-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If they testify, we will ask them, but I am not able to put these questions to them. But I'm asking you as a witness before this Tribunal, and I'm asking you. Please respond. If you know yes or no, you have to tell me yes or no. Is it logical that you, as a user, fill in the number of pages without that being done by the person who issued the note-book to you in the first place?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: I really don't want to enter into any kind of discussion with you about this, sir, whether I can receive such a document or not and whether I should or shouldn't do that, because I said that I did receive an order that I was the one who should fill in the number of pages. So I simply executed the order that I was given. As for the policies of the command, I said a number of times that I was never at the command, I am not familiar with their practices and policy, and this is an item that I received and the command that I received at the facility when the book was empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, were these note-books burned while you were on location or were they used for other purposes, such as heating, because we've heard testimony to that effect as well?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: I think that issue has been clarified. There was a period when we did not have books, we were not getting note-books from the command, and the papers we were using we did not have to give to anyone. They were considered worthless. So what you said about the burning of papers, I don't know if it was for heating, but certainly to start a fire, they could have been used for that purpose. But the note-books that we have before us now have not been burned and have not been used for starting a fire. Each of the note-books that were given to the location were later turned over to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Why suddenly -- why did these materials written in the note-books suddenly become valuable, whereas earlier they had been considered worthless? Was it somebody's decision?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: I can answer the question in part only. Quite simply, an order came that note-books would be used, that note-books would be provided from the command, that we need to archive them and return them to the command once they were filled.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you acquire these note-books yourselves?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: No, sir. The note-books were delivered to me in the course of rotation, when we changed shifts. At the location, logistical support was given on the same occasion. We would turn over the note-books that were used up, and audio-recordings, and new ones would be brought in. At the same time, we repaired four UHER devices that we had. Some were constantly in use. It was never considered important whether there were more than four UHERs in use. Four were the standard set.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: From that time when you used -- when you started using note-books, were operators able to bring their own note-books to record conversations intercepted?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: One could only do that upon orders of the command and with their approval. That means if the command was unable to supply note-books and they instead sent somebody to buy note-books.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was it possible to buy note-books somewhere close to the location? Was there a shop?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: There was a shop four kilometres away from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did they sell note-books of this kind or some other kind, paper, stationery?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: That shop sold everything they could lay their hands on. I really don't know if they had note-books as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On pages 5 and 6 of your statement, you say you had contacts with ICTY investigators, Dean Manning and Stefanie Frease, and you gave them the copies of these note-books. Can we show this statement number 434, pages 5 and 6.

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us, were you able to explain to them which intercept was recorded when, because there is not a single date in this note-book, there's only the date when it was registered by the warehouse-keeper?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: No, I did not do that. It wasn't my job to explain that, and they didn't ask me anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm reading the last sentence on page 5: "On 12 May 1999, I showed these note-books to the investigators --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The accused is saying the names unintelligibly. Could the accused please repeat and speak more slowly when he's reading?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did that. It's a copy from my own note-book that I kept myself in that period, so it's my own personal note-book. And the other three that I turned over to this Tribunal were my own personal note-books. And there is a copy of the other note-book you mentioned, where I provided copies of some of the material, is also my personal note-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm sorry. On page -- on the last page of this document, that is number 6, you say in the second paragraph: "There are details in this note-book also about the repairs of equipment and frequencies. There are also diagrams that --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot understand what the accused is reading or saying. He's speaking very, very unclearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the interpreters didn't catch what you were speaking or reading. It was quite unclear. You should speak into the microphone and perhaps indicate again from which page you are reading.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm quoting from page 6, paragraph 6. I'm not going to read it again. There's no need. I just want to ask the witness, based on what I've read so far, if he understood, why he kept these note-books that were recorded by the official authorities and they had been given numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was that appropriate or not?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: These are note-books that I kept. Some of the information was recorded even before the war. These are my personal notes that had nothing to do with the war. There are some entries of personal nature related to my family, nothing for the purposes of this Court. I focused and indicated the entries that have to do with this subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can documents be authentic that you turned over to this Tribunal while still keeping them in your personal archives? You, as operators, to what extent can they be authentic for the purposes of the Court?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: These documents had already been shown pursuant to various requests and applications, although I'm not sure whether it was in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether they are equally authentic when they are kept in personal archives as when they are when kept in official archives.

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: I'm not qualified to make that judgement, whether they would be more authentic if they had been kept by official authorities. But in any case, they couldn't be, because they contain personal information that has nothing to do with this institution or the events of this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But you say from them, you let this Tribunal have part of the material that is relevant; is that so?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: Yes, that is so. The pages are marked, and the part of the note-book that can be shared has been marked, and everyone was happy with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Then tell me, what is the purpose of putting numbers on this note-book and assigning certain numbers when everyone can use them for their own personal archives?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: The only thing I was asked was, from the day when entries started in this note-book, the material that has been copied, that I put in no further personal information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I just wanted to make it clear from the record, because the accused's question is conflating clearly two different sets of note-books that this witness has made abundantly clear, I think, in his answers that there are personal note-books and then there are the intercept note-books. And without distinguishing between the two, the accused is referring to one and the other and conflating the two. I think the witness has managed to keep them straight, but I want, if there are going to be further questions along this line, that the accused make specific reference to whether he's referring to the personal note-books or the intercept note-books about which we heard the testimony about registering them, numbering the page numbers, whereas with the personal note-books there has been no such testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, you said a moment ago you had been told to put in no further personal information into the note-books?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Until that time, were you allowed to make your own notes in these note-books?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were you able to add or change statements in the note-books until the time when you were told not to?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: We have to make a clear distinction, whether I was able to and whether I actually did. The material shown here has not been tampered with in any way. I didn't add anything. I was able to put in lists of my own supplies because I was running my own business, et cetera. It has nothing to do with the other information contained. But I stopped doing that at a certain point when I was told to stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the note-books shown here under the tab in the binder that you received from the Prosecutor, the intercepts, are there any telegrams that another person started recording and then you took over?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question. Is it in my note-books? Could you repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'll read out to you the last sentence from page 6: "The start of this entry was made by another operator, whom I may have relieved so he could prepare lunch or leave the shift. This entry is entitled 'CX 3, 11.19,' and the entry which relates to the commencement of that book is 14 July 1995." Can you clarify this, if you didn't understand my previous question?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that text now before me: First of all, a small correction. It's not "CX," as you said, it's "CH," and it's not the time that you've said. It's 11.19. Yes, I made this entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And who put in the date, "14 July 1995"?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is that the date when the note-book was first put into use or is it the date of some particular intercept?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: Sir, if you want to discuss this text, I'd like to see the handwritten version. I want to be sure what exactly you're asking and what it refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You can ask the Prosecutor if he can give you that, because he must have that in the supporting material. I don't have it. Are there any entries in this note-book that were started by one operator and continued by you?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I had to take a moment to look at the text to understand your question. So you're not talking any more about my note-books; you are talking about a passage from my statement. What is written there in that part of the statement is "14 July 1995." When I was giving the statement, the date from that note-book was read out. I suppose that note-book is available.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: For the record, answer the question. In this binder that you have in front of you, is there an intercept that you recorded and transcribed from a certain point in the intercept, which was started by another operator whom you relieved at some point?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: Give me a moment to find it. I cannot find it in the file that I have in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You stated here on page 6, in the last sentence, that another operator started "whom I may be relieved so he could prepare lunch or leave the shift." That's the one-but-last sentence on page 6 in your statement. Where is that; can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: I can -- I suppose I have an idea in which book it should be, but I don't have this material here with me. But I did present this material, and this is my statement. This is, indeed, what I said. And there is an intercept where you can see, really, that until halfway down the text, the handwriting is not mine.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see that the accused is returning to this issue of this intercept that's referred to in the witness statement here at the end of the last page in the English. If the accused wishes to have that original intercept note-book brought in, and again that's a different note-book from the one that's in the witness's binder altogether - this is something that was just discussed in the witness statement - we're happy to do that. We were not given any list of cross-examination materials from the Defence, so we don't have every single intercept note-book here with us. We only have that which we put on our list. But if the general wants that, we can certainly clarify this issue very quickly if this witness is shown that particular document, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, Mr. Thayer is indicating that you perhaps mix up two different note-books, and that could create some problems.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'm not confusing those note-books. I'm talking about note-book number 97, and the witness also talks about it in his statement. I quote: "I recognised my handwriting." That's on page 6, the last paragraph but one: "I recognised my handwriting in some of the note-books, including an entry in the note-book which is marked '97' on the cover, an RRU 800, as well as the date, '14 July 1995.' My handwriting appears in one number of entries, including one at the bottom of page 7 which goes on to the next page. The beginning of that entry was made by another operator whom I perhaps relieved so he could prepare lunch or leave the shift: This entry is headed "CH 3 11.19," and the entry which marks the commencement of that book is '14 July 1995.'" End of witness statement. I'm just asking what the witness has stated and which has been used as evidence. Can that be a reliable piece of evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Have we seen the note-book number 97 today in court --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- or number 9, as I recall it?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I repeat, Mr. President. These are two different note-books. The general asked the witness to look in the note-book that he was given today to find an intercept that is a different intercept from a different note-book that's referred to in the statement. We are happy to bring in note-book 97, as Your Honour has pointed out, which is a different note-book from number 9, which is what the witness was shown today. If the general wishes that to be brought in, we're happy to comply. But we've had no notice, so we don't have it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We are now running out of time. We have to come to an end because the courtroom will be used by another trial in half an hour. Could you -- this problem could be resolved, I think, until the hearing of tomorrow. Could you please indicate, Mr. Tolimir, how long your remainder of the cross-examination will be?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have only two more questions, and then I'm finished, if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That could be helpful. But do you accept the explanation about the two different note-books by Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't accept or reject anything. I'm just asking about certain things that are illogical concerning a piece of evidence given and offered in this courtroom. I don't want to discuss it; I just want to ask the witness if there had been any proceedings against him while he was working in the northern location.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where he was where? Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The northern location?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: Now I heard. No, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you involved in burglaring [as interpreted] the UNPROFOR antennas while you were there?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did the UNPROFOR have their antennas there at the location?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: They had their transmitter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did NATO have their transmitter there?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: Not that I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you turn the antennas around or did antennas, themselves, choose channels?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: No, we turned them manually.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Why, when the antenna was able to do scanning and select channels where conversations were going on?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: Can you just repeat the first thing you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you have scanning devices?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: Yes. But what you asked me a moment ago was why we turned antennas manually when the device was able to scan. Is that what you asked?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, I asked that, but later I asked if you had scanning devices.

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: Yes, we had scanning devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: These scanning devices, do they make it unnecessary for operators to turn antennas around if they're able to find frequencies and channels themselves?

utterances.speaker: PW-033
utterances.text: No, sir. That's something the rotator does.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat. This question was not heard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, since we did not use a rotator, it depends on the performance of the equipment. I'm talking about the technical capacities of the rotator. In some devices, it is set up so that it self-activates at a certain level of signal. Such devices exist, but we didn't have them. We used the devices where we would fix antennas ourselves, and we would use them to scan one direction, one route.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. Thank everyone who helped hear this witness. I have finished my examination, and I will clear up other issues through my examination of other witnesses, and that will not affect the quality of examination, and we will be able to get all the information we need. Thank you, Witness. God bless you. Thank the interpreters and everyone who helped us complete this examination today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Thayer, is there any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, you will be pleased to hear that this concludes the examination, and you are now free to return to your normal activities. Thank you for attending here in The Hague, and we wish you a safe journey back. Thank you very much. But please be seated for a moment. Mr. Thayer, in the meantime, I got the information that the Prosecution intends to call Witness Stanko Gojkovic tomorrow first. Is that the fact, because there were some changes?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President. That is the Prosecution's intention, subject, of course, to the Trial Chamber's decision regarding our motion to convert him from a 92 bis witness to a 92 ter witness. We note that -- I believe that the Defence did not object to that. Obviously, having him here for cross-examination is something they're looking forward to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Chamber has considered your motion. The motion is granted, and we hope that you follow the guide-lines of the Chamber, how to proceed with the exhibits and the transcripts, which should be the corrected and official one. The same relates to the witness who was still present. I didn't ask you earlier today if these are the official and corrected transcripts of the Popovic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We have confirmation from the source, Mr. President, that they are official.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That is very helpful. Thank you very much for your patience. We adjourn and resume tomorrow at 9.00 in this courtroom. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 16th day of June, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.52 p.m.,
